nodes.body: {~HERO:Vera~} stepped onto the platform just as the sleet began its slow turn to snow. The flakes fell fat and unhurried, catching in the wool of her collar and melting against the station clock, which had already stopped at ten past eleven—though whether tonight, last week, or years ago, she could not have said. The last northbound overnight train of the season waited at the platform like a breath held too long, its windows amber-lit and fogged with the heat of other travellers. No whistle sounded. No guard called the departure. The snow was already burying the rails behind her, and the only thing moving in the whole station was the minute hand on {~HERO:Vera~}'s own watch, still ticking. She climbed aboard.

choices.label: Find a seat and take it in.

nodes.body: The carriage was half-empty and entirely strange. Vera stood in the aisle, one hand on a seat-back to steady herself against the sway, and felt the train arrange itself around her like a house she had once dreamed. Four corridors unreeled from where she stood: one toward the soft chime of a clock being punched, another past drawn sleeper curtains the colour of old tea, a third toward a folded square of paper lying alone on an empty seat, and the last to the dark window where the black country slid soundlessly by. The overhead lamps buzzed faintly, and somewhere further down the train a child laughed once and did not laugh again.

{~HERO:Vera~} moved toward the small, steady sound of the punch-clock. It was a silvery click, rhythmic as a heartbeat and just as private. The night conductor stood at the vestibule end of the carriage, a tall man in an old blue serge uniform. He turned the brass key of his clock with the absent care of someone who had done it ten thousand times. The carriage swayed, and {~HERO:Vera~} caught her own reflection in the cold glass behind him. A pale face hung over the rushing dark, her features doubled by the lamplight and the snow. She was about to turn away when she noticed it. The conductor's hands did not cast a shadow on the wall behind him, though everything else in the corridor did.

{~HERO:Vera~} stepped nearer. The corridor lamps guttered as the train took a long curve, and the conductor's silver punch-clock swung on its chain, catching the light in a way that seemed independent of any source. He had not looked at her yet, but the angle of his jaw told her he knew she was there. She could cross the remaining distance between them and ask her question plainly—risk the notice of a man whose shadow had abandoned him, and whatever that attention might cost. Or she could settle into the seat nearest the vestibule and watch him work through the long hours, patient as the track unwinding beneath them, trusting that the train would reveal its strangeness in its own time.

{~HERO:Vera~} crossed the remaining steps and spoke before she could lose her nerve. The conductor turned to her with a stillness that was not unfriendly but was not entirely human either, and when she asked why the platform clock had stopped, he answered in a voice as dry as ticket-stubs: "It hasn't stopped. It's waiting." He did not explain what it was waiting for, and he turned back to his punch-clock before she could ask a second question, but the words lodged in her chest like a stone dropped into deep water. The train was not running late. The train was running toward something that had not yet decided to arrive.

{~HERO:Vera~} chose the window seat nearest the vestibule, tucked her feet up beneath her, and did not look away. The conductor moved through his work with strange precision: punching the clock, checking the corridor lamps, running a thumb along each door's edge. It was the care of someone who had been at it far longer than any timetable could explain. The night deepened around the carriage, and the train's rocking grew hypnotic, pulling at the edges of her being awake. She could hold onto her unease and carry it forward into the later hours. Or she could let the steady rhythm close over her and sleep without having understood.

choices.label: Hold the thread and go on.

nodes.body: The train pushed on into the snow, and the wrongness that {~HERO:Vera~} had glimpsed would not leave her alone. The conductor's hands, shadowless against the wall. His clock, waiting. The whole corridor seemed to lean toward that small, silvery absence as though it were the centre around which the night turned. She could feel the journey drawing tight around her, every passenger in their compartment, every curtain drawn, the whole carriage holding its breath. Something on this train was unfinished, and she was no longer sure it was only the journey.

{~HERO:Vera~} rose and moved deeper into the train, the conductor's words still settling in her like snow against glass. "It's waiting." The cars swayed beneath her, and the connecting doors between carriages opened with a sigh of colder air, each new corridor a little darker, a little quieter, until she was walking through a silence so complete that the clack of the wheels seemed to come from somewhere outside the train entirely. Ahead, she could sense it building—a question the whole train seemed constructed to ask, a single inquiry that every passenger, every drawn curtain, every stopped clock was leaning toward. She followed the lean.

She held on as long as she could, but the train's rhythm was older than her resolve. The sway of the carriage deepened into something soft and tidal, and before {~HERO:Vera~} could fix the conductor's strangeness into a thought she could carry, sleep took her. When she woke, the corridor was empty of him, his clock silent, the window showing only the faintest grey at the horizon's edge. She had slept through the moment—the one sharp instant when she might have understood—and now she was left with nothing but her own reflection in the cold glass, whole and unharmed and scraped hollow by the thing she had almost grasped.

{~HERO:Vera~} pushed through into the sleeper car and the air changed at once. It was warmer, closer, smelling of wool blankets and old lavender and something faintly metallic beneath, like the taste of a coin. The long row of curtained berths stretched ahead of her, each one drawn tight. Their heavy fabric was the colour of steeped tea, moving slightly with the train's motion, though no breath stirred behind them. The carriage swayed and {~HERO:Vera~} caught her own reflection in the cold glass of the nearest compartment door. A pale face hung over the rushing dark. She was about to turn away when she noticed it: every sleeper curtain was drawn from the inside.

{~HERO:Vera~} walked the narrow aisle between the berths. The runner carpet muffled her steps. The silence behind each curtain was not the silence of sleep but the silence of listening. From the berth at the far end, a single thread of colder air seeped through a gap where the curtain did not quite meet the wall. She could stop there and pull the curtain aside, risk whatever waited behind it, and demand an answer from the dark. Or she could take the seat halfway down the aisle and let the sleeper car keep its counsel, patient as the mountain tunnel somewhere ahead, trusting the curtain would part when the night was ready.

{~HERO:Vera~} stopped at the last berth and drew the curtain aside in one motion, her heart high in her throat. The berth was empty. Not empty as though the passenger had stepped away—the blankets were folded, the pillow smooth, the window behind it showing only the snow and the dark—but empty as though no one had ever been assigned to sleep there, despite the drawn curtain and the slip of paper tucked into the reading lamp's clip. {~HERO:Vera~} lifted the slip. On it, in a handwriting that looked exactly like her own, was written a single word: "Wait." She had never seen the note before. She was certain she had written it.

{~HERO:Vera~} lowered herself into the aisle seat halfway along the sleeper car and let the drawn curtains keep their vigil. The train's motion rocked through her bones, and the gathering quiet was broken only by the occasional soft chime of the heating pipes contracting in the cold. Nothing moved behind the curtains, but the sense of being watched did not fade; it deepened, as though the berths themselves were waiting for something she had not yet done. She could keep the thread of her unease and carry it forward into the later hours, or let the steady rhythm close over her and sleep without having understood.

choices.label: Hold the thread and go on.

nodes.body: Whichever she had carried from the sleeper car, the note or the watching silence, it had planted itself in {~HERO:Vera~}'s mind and would not leave. Every drawn curtain she passed on her way back seemed to lean toward her. The corridor narrowed like a passage in a dream. The sameness of the berths was a wrongness, a repetition that belonged to no ordinary timetable. She could feel the journey drawing tight around her, every silent passenger, every flickering lamp, the whole carriage holding its breath. Something on this train was unfinished. She was no longer sure it was only the journey.

{~HERO:Vera~} buttoned her coat and walked on through the train, the word "Wait" burning small and steady in her mind like a candle left in an empty room. The cars swayed beneath her, and the connecting doors opened onto corridors that grew older with every threshold—brass fittings dulled to pewter, carpet worn to the weft, windows fogged with a frost that did not melt under her touch. Ahead, she could feel it waiting—the one query that every empty berth and every drawn curtain had been arranged to pose, the question the whole train leaned toward like a plant toward a distant window. She followed the lean.

She held on as long as she could, watching the drawn curtains ripple in a draft she could not feel. But the train's rhythm was older than her resolve. The sway of the carriage deepened into something soft and tidal. Before {~HERO:Vera~} could shape the sleeper car's strangeness into a thought she could keep, sleep took her. When she woke, the curtains were open and the berths were neatly made. The carriage was filled with the thin grey light of an hour before dawn. She had missed the moment—the one sharp instant when she might have parted the curtain and found whatever had been waiting behind it. Now she was left with nothing but the faint, fading memory of her own handwriting on a slip of paper she could no longer find.

ending.title: A Door You Did Not Open

nodes.body: {~HERO:Vera~} crossed to the empty seat and picked up the letter before she could talk herself out of it. The paper was thick and cream-coloured, folded once, with no envelope and no name on the outside. When she turned it over, the carriage swayed and she caught her own reflection in the cold glass of the window—a pale face suspended over the rushing dark, the letter a small white ghost in her hands. She was about to put it back when she noticed it: the ink on the outside fold was still faintly damp, as though the letter had been written on this train, in this seat, only moments before she boarded.

{~HERO:Vera~} sat down with the letter in her lap. The damp ink began to blur slightly at the edges where her thumb rested. The carriage lamps guttered as the train took a long curve. The handwriting inside—she could see it through the thin paper, a tight, urgent slant—seemed to shift under the light. She could unfold it now, read whatever message had been left for her, and risk the notice of a letter whose author might still be somewhere on the train. Or she could tuck it into her coat pocket and let the night carry her forward. She could be as patient as the track unwinding beneath them, trusting that the words would reveal themselves when she was ready.

{~HERO:Vera~} unfolded the letter. The handwriting was her father's—she knew it before she read a single word, the cramped lowercase and the way the 'g's dropped below the line like anchors—but her father had been dead for three winters. The message was brief, only two lines: "The north line remembers its passengers. Do not be afraid of what it remembers about you." Below that, a third line had been started and then crossed out so heavily the paper was nearly torn. {~HERO:Vera~} could not make out the words, but the force of the cancellation told her more than the sentence ever could have. Someone—her father, or whatever wore his handwriting—had wanted very badly not to say something.

{~HERO:Vera~} folded the letter back along its original crease and slipped it into her coat pocket, against her ribs. Its small weight pressed there like a held breath. She could not bring herself to read it yet—the damp ink, the emptiness of the seat where it had lain. But she could feel the message waiting for her, patient as the snow outside the window. The night deepened around the carriage. The train's motion turned hypnotic, a long rocking that pulled at the edges of her wakefulness. She could keep the thread of her unease and carry it forward into the later hours. Or she could let the steady rhythm close over her and sleep without having read the words she was already beginning to guess.

choices.label: Hold the thread and go on.

nodes.body: The letter—read or unread—had opened a door in {~HERO:Vera~}'s chest that she had kept locked for a long time. The words she had seen, or the words she had felt waiting, would not settle; they turned in her mind like a key in a lock that had rusted almost shut. The whole carriage seemed to lean toward that small folded square of paper as though it were the centre around which the night had been arranged. She could feel the journey drawing tight around her, every passenger in their compartment, every lamp burning low in its bracket, the whole train holding its breath. Something on this train was unfinished, and she was beginning to suspect it was her.

{~HERO:Vera~} stood and walked on into the train, the letter warm against her side like a living thing. "Do not be afraid," the handwriting had told her, and she tried, but the trying itself was a kind of fear. The cars swayed beneath her, and each connecting door opened onto a corridor a little narrower, a little darker, until she was walking through a silence so complete that she could hear her own pulse in her ears. Ahead, she could sense it building—a query the whole train seemed designed to ask her, a question that the letter had begun and the night would finish. She followed the unfinished sentence.

She held on as long as she could, the letter a small, insistent weight against her ribs, but the train's rhythm was older than her resolve. The sway of the carriage deepened into something soft and tidal, and before {~HERO:Vera~} could unfold the paper and read what the crossed-out line had been trying to tell her, sleep took her. When she woke, the seat beside her was empty, and the letter—the damp ink, the anchor-heavy 'g's, the two-line message and its cancelled third—was gone from her pocket. She searched the aisle, the seat cushions, the floor beneath the window, but the paper had vanished as completely as if it had never been written. She was left with nothing but the memory of her father's handwriting, and the certainty that she had let the one question that mattered slip through her fingers.

{~HERO:Vera~} turned from the aisle and pressed her forehead to the cold glass of the carriage window. Outside, the black country slid past in long, unbroken strokes: dark fields stitched with snow, stands of birch pale as bones against the treeline, the occasional distant light that belonged to no house she could imagine. The carriage swayed and her own reflection floated over the landscape, a pale face suspended above the rushing dark. She was about to pull back when she noticed it—one of those distant lights was not distant at all. It was moving with the train, keeping perfect pace alongside the track, a small yellow point that never fell behind and never pulled ahead.

{~HERO:Vera~} stayed at the window. Her breath fogged the glass and then cleared as the train pushed north into colder air. The light was still there—steady, companionable, utterly wrong. It did not move like a lantern in a farmhouse window or the headlamp of a car on a parallel road. It moved exactly as the train moved, as though it were attached to the carriage by an invisible tether. She could press her investigation further: open the window an inch and lean into the slipstream to see the light for what it truly was, risking whatever cold or strangeness rushed in. Or she could stay in her seat and watch it travel beside her, patient as the snow, trusting that the journey would explain the light when the light was ready to be explained.

{~HERO:Vera~} wrestled the window down an inch—the brass catch was stiff with cold—and the night rushed in, sharp and smelling of pine and iron and the vast, unsalted cold of the interior. The yellow light did not waver. It hung in the dark at the edge of the track bed. As the train pushed past a thinning stand of birch, {~HERO:Vera~} saw it clearly for the first time. It was a single signal lamp on a post that had no business being there. It burned a steady, impossible gold in the middle of a field that had no station, no siding, no railway building for miles. The lamp was lit and waiting and completely alone. She knew, with the sudden certainty of a child waking from a fever dream, that it was waiting for her.

{~HERO:Vera~} did not open the window. She stayed in her seat, her cheek against the cold glass, and kept the yellow light in the corner of her eye as the train carried her north. It neither approached nor receded; it simply kept pace, a small unwavering companion in the dark beyond the snow. The night deepened around the carriage, and the train's motion turned hypnotic, a long rocking that pulled at the edges of her wakefulness. She could hold the thread of her unease—the impossible lantern pacing the track—and carry it forward into the later hours, or let the steady rhythm close over her and sleep without having understood what it wanted.

choices.label: Hold the thread and go on.

nodes.body: The light—named or unnamed, faced or watched from the corner of her eye—had taken up residence in {~HERO:Vera~}'s mind and would not be dismissed. The whole landscape beyond the window now seemed arranged around that single golden point. Every field and treeline and distant farmhouse lamp bent toward it like iron filings toward a magnet. The carriage swayed and she felt the journey drawing tight around her. Every passenger in their compartment, every snowflake tracing its arc to the glass, the whole train holding its breath. Something on this train was unfinished. The light outside was a part of it—or the signal of it—or the question itself, burning in the dark.

{~HERO:Vera~} pulled her coat tighter and moved on through the train. The gold light still burned at the edge of her vision, even when she turned away from the windows. It seemed to have followed her inside—not as a visible point but as a warmth, a pressure, a sense that something beyond the glass was keeping pace with her questions. The cars swayed beneath her. Each connecting door opened onto a corridor that seemed to be waiting for her to catch up to an understanding that was already forming, patient and strange, in the dark ahead. The whole train leaned toward it—the one query the night was built to ask her—and she followed the lean.

She held on as long as she could, her eyes on the gold light that refused to fall behind, but the train's rhythm was older than her resolve. The sway of the carriage deepened into something soft and tidal, and before {~HERO:Vera~} could name what the light was or why it had chosen her window, sleep took her. When she woke, the window showed only the first grey suggestion of dawn over a ridgeline she did not recognise, and the yellow light was gone—snuffed or satisfied or simply finished with her. She had missed the moment, and now she was left with nothing but her own reflection in the cold glass and the faint, unreachable certainty that something in the dark had been trying to speak.

The dining car was warmer than the rest of the train and smelled of coffee that had been sitting on the hot plate since the afternoon departure. Four travellers sat at separate tables near the window, each one angled slightly away from the others, each with a cup of something that had long since gone cold. {~HERO:Vera~} paused in the doorway. The carriage swayed and she caught her own reflection in the dark glass of the drinks cabinet—a pale face suspended over the rows of unopened bottles. She was about to find a table of her own when she noticed it: the four travellers had not looked at their cups, or at each other, or at the window, in all the time she had been standing there.

{~HERO:Vera~} stepped into the dining car and took the table nearest the service door, where she could watch the four travellers without seeming to. They were not travellers, she realised slowly—or not only travellers. They were regulars. Their coats hung on the rack behind them with the settled look of garments that had been riding this train for longer than a single journey, and the cups before them had dried rings of old coffee layered like geological strata. She could approach the nearest of them—a woman with a brooch in the shape of a bird she could not name—and ask outright why no one was ordering and why no one was leaving. Or she could stay at her table and let the dining car keep its customs, patient as the snow outside, trusting that the regulars would speak when the night was ready for speech.

{~HERO:Vera~} crossed to the woman with the bird-shaped brooch and sat down across from her without waiting for an invitation. The woman looked up slowly, as though she had forgotten how to hurry, and her eyes were the colour of the coffee in her cup—dark and old and no longer warm. "Why don't any of you order?" {~HERO:Vera~} asked, keeping her voice low. The woman's mouth moved into something that was almost a smile. "We ordered," she said. "A long time ago. The kitchen is still working on it." She gestured toward the galley door, which {~HERO:Vera~} now saw was closed and had no handle on this side. "It's a complicated dish."

{~HERO:Vera~} stayed at her table and watched the regulars in the dark glass of the drinks cabinet. The longer she looked, the more she understood: they were not waiting for coffee. They were waiting for something that had been promised to them before she was born, a debt the train owed that it was still—after all these journeys, all these cold cups and drawn curtains—in the process of repaying. The night deepened around the dining car and the motion of the train turned hypnotic, a long rocking that pulled at the edges of her wakefulness. She could hold the thread of her observation and carry it forward into the later hours, or let the steady rhythm close over her and sleep without having understood what the regulars were owed.

nodes.body: The galley door with no handle. The coffee rings built up like sediment. The woman with the bird-brooch who had almost smiled. The wrongness had settled over the dining car like dust and would not be disturbed. {~HERO:Vera~} could feel the four regulars around her, each at their separate table, each waiting for a meal the kitchen would never finish making, and the whole carriage seemed to lean toward that closed galley door as though it were the centre around which the night had been arranged. She could feel the journey drawing tight around her, the train holding its breath. Something on this train was unfinished, and the dining-car regulars had been waiting for it longer than anyone.

{~HERO:Vera~} rose from her table—the regulars did not watch her go, but she felt their attention like a hand between her shoulder blades—and walked on through the train, carrying the image of that handleless galley door with her. The cars swayed beneath her, and each connecting door opened onto a corridor that was smaller, darker, older than the one before it, until she was walking through a silence so complete that the only sound was her own breathing and the distant, rhythmic snick of a punch-clock she could not locate. Ahead, she could feel the question gathering—the one inquiry every passenger seemed to be riding toward, the centre the whole train was built around. She followed the lean.

{~HERO:Vera~} stayed at her table long enough to feel the dining car's particular stillness settle into her bones. The regulars did not speak and did not move, but the woman with the bird-brooch caught her eye once before {~HERO:Vera~} rose to leave, and in that glance was an acknowledgment—not an explanation, but a recognition that {~HERO:Vera~} had seen something true. The kitchen galley door stayed closed. The coffee stayed cold. But {~HERO:Vera~} walked out of the dining car carrying the certainty that the four travellers were not passengers at all, but something more like witnesses, and that she had been permitted to sit among them for a little while. She did not know what they were witnessing, but the knowledge was hers now, small and hard and real.

{~HERO:Vera~} heard the child before she saw her—a soft, tuneless humming from the far end of the carriage, where the corridor lamps had been dimmed to a single amber glow. The child sat cross-legged on a seat near the rear vestibule, a small figure in a coat too large for her, her hair escaping from a braid that had been done hours ago and never retied. The carriage swayed and {~HERO:Vera~} caught her own reflection in the cold glass above the child's head: a pale face suspended over the rushing dark. She was about to move on when she noticed it—the child was not looking out the window or down at a book but directly at {~HERO:Vera~}, as though she had been waiting for her to arrive.

{~HERO:Vera~} walked the length of the carriage and took the seat across the aisle from the child, who watched her approach without blinking. Up close, the child was younger than {~HERO:Vera~} had first thought—seven, perhaps, or eight—but her eyes were the eyes of someone who had been awake for a very long time, and there was a stillness in her small face that belonged to the very old or the very lost. She could lean across the aisle and ask the child directly why she was alone on the last train north, why she was not sleeping, what she knew about the stopped clock and the handleless galley door. Or she could stay in her seat and let the child keep her own counsel, patient as the snow, trusting that whatever the girl knew, she would share it when the night was ready.

{~HERO:Vera~} leaned across the aisle. "Are you travelling alone?" The child considered the question with the gravity of a much older person, her small hands folded in the lap of the too-large coat. "Everyone on this train is travelling alone," she said. "That's the rule. You can only board if you're going toward something you can't carry with you." She said it as a fact, the way another child might recite the days of the week, and then she turned to look out the window at the snow, and {~HERO:Vera~} understood that the conversation was over, and that the child had given her more than she had any right to expect—a rule, a condition, a door that swung open onto a much larger dark.

{~HERO:Vera~} did not speak. She stayed in her seat across the aisle and watched the child in the dark glass of the window, where both their reflections floated over the snow. The girl did not seem to mind being watched; she simply resumed her quiet humming, a melody {~HERO:Vera~} almost recognised but could not place, as though it belonged to a lullaby she had heard once in very early childhood. The night deepened around the carriage and the train's motion turned hypnotic, a long rocking that pulled at the edges of her wakefulness. She could hold the thread of her curiosity—the child who never slept, the melody she half-knew—and carry it forward into the later hours, or let the steady rhythm close over her and sleep without having heard what the girl might say if she were asked.

nodes.body: The rule the child had spoken—or the rule {~HERO:Vera~} had felt waiting behind her silence—had opened a door in the night that would not close again. You can only board if you're going toward something you can't carry with you. The words turned in {~HERO:Vera~}'s mind like a key in a lock, and she understood, with a clarity that was almost physical, that every passenger in every compartment was riding toward a burden they had left behind, and that the train was not carrying them north so much as carrying them away from something they could no longer hold. She could feel the journey drawing tight around her, the whole train holding its breath. Something was unfinished, and the child knew what it was.

{~HERO:Vera~} stood and walked on through the train, carrying the child's words like a small smooth stone in her pocket. "You can only board if you're going toward something you can't carry with you." The cars swayed beneath her, and each connecting door opened onto a corridor that seemed to be asking her, silently, what she was riding away from—and what she hoped to find at the north terminus that she could not carry now. She walked deeper into the dark, and the question gathered ahead of her, patient and immense, the one inquiry the whole train had been built to ask. She followed it.

{~HERO:Vera~} stayed in her seat until the child's humming stopped, and when it did, the silence that followed was not empty but full—full of something that had been said without words, a communication that passed between them in the amber glow of the dimmed lamps. The girl did not turn around again, and {~HERO:Vera~} did not ask another question, but as she rose to leave the carriage she understood that she had been given something: not an answer, but a key. The child knew things about this train that no adult passenger would ever speak aloud, and {~HERO:Vera~} had been allowed to sit beside that knowledge for a little while. It did not complete the picture, but it was true, and it was hers, and it went with her into the darker cars ahead.

{~HERO:Vera~} found him in the vestibule between cars, a gaunt man in an overcoat that had been patched at the elbows with fabric that did not quite match. He was facing the window—or what would have been a window, if the glass had not been so thickly frosted over—and his lips were moving, a soft murmur that rose and fell with the rhythm of the wheels. The carriage swayed and {~HERO:Vera~} caught her own reflection in the brass plate beside the door handle: a pale face suspended over the rushing dark. She was about to pass him when she noticed it—the man was counting, a low chant of station names that {~HERO:Vera~} had never heard before, places that belonged to no line and no timetable she recognised.

{~HERO:Vera~} stopped in the vestibule and let the connecting door close behind her, sealing them both in the cold, rattling space between carriages. The man did not acknowledge her, but his counting neither quickened nor slowed; it simply continued, a steady litany of names that sounded like they belonged to villages that had been erased from the map a century ago. She could step into his line of sight and ask him outright what he was counting, why the stations never came, whether he had been riding this train long enough to know the answer to the question it was asking. Or she could lean against the opposite wall and listen, patient as the snow outside, trusting that the litany would tell her what she needed to know without a single word exchanged.

"What are you counting?" {~HERO:Vera~} asked, stepping into the man's line of sight. He stopped mid-syllable and looked at her—not through her or past her but directly into her face, with an attention so sudden and so complete that she took half a step back. "I am counting the stations this train used to stop at," he said. His voice was dry and precise, like a schoolmaster's. "Before they were removed from the timetable. Before they were removed from the maps. Before they were removed from the remembering of everyone who ever disembarked there." He paused. "There are a great many of them. I have been counting for some time." He did not say how long, and {~HERO:Vera~} did not ask.

{~HERO:Vera~} did not interrupt him. She leaned against the cold wall of the vestibule and let the litany wash over her—name after name after name, a geography of absence rolling past in the man's quiet, unstoppable voice. The stations he named had been real once, she was suddenly sure of it, real places where real passengers had stood on real platforms and waited for a train that was exactly this one, and the man was keeping them alive by the simple, impossible act of remembering. The night deepened around the vestibule and the motion of the train turned hypnotic, a long rocking that pulled at the edges of her wakefulness. She could hold the thread of his counting and carry it forward into the later hours, or let the steady rhythm close over her and sleep without having counted the names herself.

choices.label: Hold the thread and go on.

nodes.body: The man's list of names had stuck in {~HERO:Vera~}'s mind—all those lost stations, all those stops rubbed off the maps, still riding in the memory of one thin passenger in a patched coat. The wrongness was huge and quiet: a whole hidden world, carried north through the snow by a train that no longer stopped there. She felt the trip tighten around her. The walls of the vestibule seemed to lean in toward the man's soft, steady voice. The whole train held its breath. Something was not finished—not just the trip, but the world itself, full of places forgotten by everyone except this one keeper of names.

{~HERO:Vera~} pushed through the far door of the vestibule and walked on into the train, the names the man had spoken still cycling through her mind like a prayer she had not meant to memorise. The cars swayed beneath her, and each connecting door opened onto a corridor that seemed a little less substantial than the one before it, as though the train itself were thinning out the further north it travelled. Ahead, she could feel the question gathering—the one inquiry that every passenger was riding toward, the one answer that every erased station and every stopped clock had been arranged to point at. She followed the pointing.

{~HERO:Vera~} stayed in the vestibule long enough to hear the man finish one full round of his list and start again from the top. In that repeat, she found a shape she could hold: the names were not random. They were ordered by how far they were from the southern end—a map of loss that followed the line north, station by station, until they hit a place even he could not name. {~HERO:Vera~} found her in the last room before the luggage car. A woman sat alone in a pool of lamplight that seemed to bend toward her, as if even the light was being careful. {~HERO:Vera~} found the conductor again in the front vestibule of the second-to-last carriage, standing exactly as he had stood before—tall and blue and shadowless—but something in the angle of his shoulders had changed. The mountain tunnel was close now; she could feel it in the pressure of the air, in the way the train's whistle had begun to sound longer and lower, a note that slid down the scale and did not come back up. The carriage swayed and {~HERO:Vera~} caught her own reflection in the cold glass of the door panel: a pale face suspended over the rushing dark. She was about to call out to him when she noticed it—his silver punch-clock was no longer ticking. The hands had stopped, and he was not winding it.

{~HERO:Vera~} stepped into the vestibule and let the door close behind her, cutting off the warmer air of the carriage. {~HERO:Vera~} stepped into his line of sight and asked the question she had been carrying since the platform clock had stopped: "Where is this train going?" The conductor looked at her for a long moment, and then he did something she had not seen him do before: he smiled. It goes through a place—the same place, over and over—until every passenger is ready to get off. The terminus is not a station. The terminus is a condition." He touched the stopped clock at his belt. {~HERO:Vera~} did not press him. nodes.body: {~HERO:Vera~} saw the signal lamps through the forward window of the dining car—three bright points of colour suspended in the dark ahead of the mountain tunnel's mouth. The train slowed as it approached the grade, and the wheels beneath her began to sound different, a heavier rhythm that seemed to press down on the rails as though the track were climbing into thinner air. The carriage swayed and {~HERO:Vera~} caught her own reflection in the cold glass: a pale face suspended over the rushing dark. She was about to settle back into her seat when she noticed it—the leftmost signal lamp was not red or green or amber but white, a steady colourless blaze that belonged to no railway she had ever seen.

{~HERO:Vera~} pressed closer to the window and cupped her hands around her eyes to block the reflection of the carriage lamps. The three signal lights burned ahead of the tunnel: red, green, and that impossible white. The red and green were the standard signals she knew—stop and proceed—but the white lamp did not belong to any code she had learned. It did not flicker in the wind. It did not seem to be attached to a post or a gantry. It simply hung in the dark above the tunnel mouth, steady and patient, and {~HERO:Vera~} understood that it was not a signal for the engineer. It was a signal for the passengers. She could study it until she understood what it was telling her, risk missing the moment when the train reached the tunnel and the choice it demanded. Or she could accept that some signals were not meant to be decoded from a distance and wait, patient as the snow, for the lamp to reveal its meaning when the train was close enough to pass beneath it.

{~HERO:Vera~} kept her eyes on the white lamp as the train climbed the grade toward the tunnel, and as the distance closed she saw what she had not been able to see from further away: the lamp was not burning. It was reflecting. Something inside the tunnel—something that lay just beyond the mouth, in the dark where the rails disappeared—was shining out through the lamp's glass with a light that had no colour and no warmth and no source that she could name. It was the light of arrival, she thought suddenly—not the arrival at a station but the arrival at the moment when a journey stopped being a passage and became something else. And the train was carrying her directly toward it.

{~HERO:Vera~} stayed at the window and watched the three lamps grow larger as the train climbed toward the tunnel. The white light did not change; it simply waited, steady and patient, as though it had been burning—or reflecting—since before the north line was laid, and would continue to burn after every passenger aboard had reached their terminus. She understood, without being able to say why, that the lamp was not a warning. It was an invitation. The night deepened around the carriage and the motion of the train slowed, the wheels dragging now against the grade. She could hold the thread of the white light and carry it forward into the tunnel, or let the steady rhythm close over her and sleep without having accepted whatever invitation the lamp was extending.

The passengers had gathered in the dining car without any signal that {~HERO:Vera~} could discern—as though the train itself had summoned them, or as though they had all arrived at the same understanding at the same moment. {~HERO:Vera~} leaned forward and spoke into the silence: "Tell me what this train is." nodes.body: {~HERO:Vera~} found the conductor standing in the open doorway of the front vestibule, the cold air streaming past him and the mountain tunnel a vast dark mouth less than half a mile ahead. He had put away his silver punch-clock—she did not know where, and the absence of it made him look smaller, more human, a man in a worn blue uniform rather than a figure out of a station clock's dream. The carriage swayed and {~HERO:Vera~} caught her own reflection in the cold glass of the door panel: a pale face suspended over the rushing dark. She was about to call out to him when she noticed it—he was not waiting for her to ask a question. He was waiting for permission to speak.

{~HERO:Vera~} stepped into the vestibule and stood beside him, the wind from the open door pulling at her hair. The conductor did not turn toward her, but when he spoke his voice was different—lower, slower, as though he were choosing each word from a very small store of words he was permitted to use. "I have been the conductor of this train for longer than you have been alive," he said. "I have seen thousands of passengers board at the southern platform. I have seen far fewer disembark at the northern terminus. The tunnel decides. I do not decide. But I can tell you what I know, if you want to hear it, before we reach the mouth." The offer hung in the cold air between them. She could take it—demand the whole truth, whatever it cost him to tell it. Or she could shake her head and let him keep his silence, patient as the stopped clock, trusting that she already knew enough.

"Tell me," {~HERO:Vera~} said. The conductor closed his eyes for a moment—the first human gesture she had seen him make—and when he opened them again, he was looking not at her but at the tunnel mouth, growing larger in the forward windows. "The north line was built for the bereaved," he said. "Not the recently bereaved—the ones who have been carrying their grief for so long it has become part of them. The train gives them a night to hold it, to name it, to decide whether they are ready to set it down. The tunnel is the threshold. If you pass through it still carrying what you boarded with, you will ride the north line forever, like the regulars in the dining car. If you pass through it empty, you will arrive at the north terminus—not a station, but a condition—and you will walk off this train into a life you have not yet lived."

"I don't need to know," {~HERO:Vera~} said, and the conductor nodded once, slowly, as though she had given him a gift. "Most people want to know," he said. "Most people ask. But the knowing doesn't change what happens in the tunnel. You carry what you carry, and you let go of what you can let go of, and the train does the rest." He fell silent, and the wind from the open door wrapped around them both, cold and clean and smelling of the high mountain snow. The night deepened around the vestibule and the motion of the train slowed, the wheels dragging now against the steepening grade. She could hold the thread of his silence and carry it forward into the tunnel, or let the steady rhythm close over her and sleep without having heard the words he was not permitted to speak.

nodes.body: The train climbed higher. The snow outside thinned to a fine, dry powder that hissed against the glass. Vera began to understand the passengers were not just fellow riders. The gold light was filling the carriage now, warm and clean, and the stopped clocks on the corridor walls did not trouble her any longer. They were not broken; they were waiting, and she was waiting with them, and the waiting itself had become its own kind of arrival. She had ridden the last northbound train of the season with open eyes and an open heart, and the journey had asked her to carry her grief and then, gently, to set it down. She had done the work. The work was finished. The train would carry her northward into the morning, and she would ride it as long as it chose to run.

The seat beside the woman in grey was warm. {~HERO:Vera~} could feel it from the aisle, a small pocket of heat in the cold carriage, as if the woman's long grief had finally begun to let go. The woman was still looking at the ridgeline, her empty hands open at her sides, and there was room beside her for one more passenger. {~HERO:Vera~} could sit down and stay with her through the tunnel and the dawn and whatever lay beyond both. The price of staying was that her own arrival would be delayed, her own letting-go postponed, the journey lengthened by the weight of another traveller's burden. Or she could step back and keep her own arrival, her own free passage through the gold light, and let the woman ride on alone.

{~HERO:Vera~} turned to the grey window and spoke the names aloud. She said her father's name, and Rowan Gate, and the north terminus that was not a station but a condition. She spoke her own grief, which she had carried so long she had forgotten its weight. The carriage was empty, or felt empty, but the words needed no one to hear them. The naming of them was its own kind of arrival—a station built from syllables, a door opening not onto a platform but onto an understanding. She had ridden the night and asked its questions. She had arrived at last at the one truth the train had been waiting to teach her. Some things cannot be carried, and some things must be spoken, and the journey north is the long, slow work of learning which is which.

{~HERO:Vera~} asked the train for nothing but a safe waking. Not the truth, not the terminus, not the name of the thing she had been carrying since the southern platform—only the quiet assurance that she would open her eyes in the morning, unharmed and whole, and that the night would not have taken anything from her that she was not ready to give. The train, being kinder than she had feared, granted exactly that and no more. It did not give her the answer to the question it had been asking. It did not show her the cancelled line in her father's letter or the station marked with her own name in the endless timetable. It simply carried her northward into the dawn and set her down, gently, at a quiet station where the clocks had started again and the snow had stopped falling.

{~HERO:Vera~} stayed on the train. She did not get off at the next station, or the one after that, or the one after that—the stations came and went, ordinary platforms with ordinary clocks and passengers who were only passengers, and still she stayed. The gold light had settled into the carriage like a permanent resident, and the stopped clocks had started again, ticking in their old familiar rhythm, and somewhere in the long morning hours she had let go of the grief she had been carrying. Not all at once—it was not a dramatic letting-go, not a revelation or a crisis—but slowly, the way snow melts from a windowsill, a little at a time, until the glass is clear and the light comes through. The north terminus was still an hour away. It would always be an hour away. And {~HERO:Vera~}, riding the last northbound train of the season with open eyes and an open heart, had finally made peace with the distance.

{~HERO:Vera~} sat down beside the woman in grey and did not get up again. The train carried them both through the morning past the ridgeline, the gold peaks, and the ordinary stations where ordinary passengers began their ordinary days. The woman did not speak much, but her hands had finally stopped holding the shape of a burden. They rested on her knees now, open and still. The train slowed at a small northern platform that {~HERO:Vera~} did not recognise. The woman rose, straightened her grey dress, and looked at {~HERO:Vera~} with an expression that was not a smile but was, in its quiet way, a thank you. She stepped down onto the platform and walked toward the station without looking back. {~HERO:Vera~} understood she had done what the train had asked. She had helped another traveller home, and the helping had turned out to be the arrival she had been riding toward all along.

{~HERO:Vera~} stayed beside the woman in grey through the morning and into the afternoon. The sun climbed the sky and began its slow descent toward the western peaks, and still she stayed. The woman did not ask her to remain. She did not ask for anything. Her empty hands were still open in her lap. But {~HERO:Vera~} could not bring herself to rise and walk away. The good deed had become a weight of its own, a second burden laid beside the first. By the time the woman stepped down at a small northern platform, {~HERO:Vera~} was worn thin and far from herself. Her own letting-go had been postponed so long she had forgotten what she had meant to set down. The train carried her onward into the dusk as she sat alone in the quiet carriage, knowing she had helped a fellow traveller but not knowing whether the cost had been more than she could afford.

{~HERO:Vera~} spoke the names into the grey glass—her father, Rowan Gate, the north line, the platform clock, the child who never slept, the woman in grey, the grief she had been carrying for so long it had become invisible to her—and the speaking of them was like uncoupling a long train of cars, one by one, until only the locomotive was left. She did not stay on the train. At the next station—a small platform in a town she did not recognise, with a clock that showed the correct time—she stepped down and stood in the ordinary morning light and watched the last northbound train of the season pull away without her. She did not mind. She had learned what she needed to learn, and the knowing had settled something in her that had been unsettled for years. The journey was over, and she had named its names, and the names would stay with her—not as a burden but as a map, a record of the passage she had made.

{~HERO:Vera~} woke at her own quiet station, the one she had been riding toward since she boarded at the southern platform, and the morning was ordinary and the clocks were running and the snow had stopped. She was unharmed. The train had kept its promise. But as she stood on the platform and watched the last northbound train of the season disappear into the grey morning, she felt the weight of the unasked questions settle into her chest like stones. The night was unexplained. The passengers were gone. The letter in her pocket was blank—the ink vanished, the map erased, the cancelled line illegible again. She had asked for safety and she had received it, but the safety came with a shadow: the sense of a door she had chosen not to walk through, a truth she had not been ready to hear, a journey she had completed without ever arriving.
